c09a0b9750: Pixel Studio Vocal Lab｜Pop singing handbook and lesson plans for six lessons
93786a8444: Six lessons of 120 minutes each. The route starts from "understanding the voice", passes through the three elements of breath, resonance and phonation, and ends at "finding a key that's your own". Every lesson follows the same rhythm: a pre-class survey shows where students are, the lesson moves through four parts (open, build, turn, close), and practice after class carries into the next lesson.
6821545e4d: Many students like to play while they sing, so every lesson's song practice leaves room for playing and singing; those who don't play can be accompanied by the teacher or a classmate.

Warm-up poll: students take turns naming a singer and song they like; the teacher types them in live and plays the song with the most votes on an instrument. Icebreaker "chorus relay": everyone sings one line of the chorus of their favourite song. The teacher then sings the same line in three tones (breathy, nasal, full resonance) and asks students to think about why the same person singing the same line can sound so different.

Students hum the same note in the middle of the room and in a corner and write down the difference. 05c50dfb6e: The six pie charts pass the baton in order: sound is first "made", then "amplified", then "heard"; the singer uses the "three elements of singing" to turn sound into singing, places it within the "three elements of music", and finally takes the stage with the "three marks of a good lead singer".
791e230a81: **1. The basics of how sound is made**
fd2adda164: **Amplitude**: how big the vibration is, which sets the volume. The more force the breath puts on the vocal folds, the bigger the amplitude.
e2183f7147: **Frequency**: how many times it vibrates per second, which sets the pitch. Concert A4 is 440 vibrations per second (440 Hz), and an octave higher is double that, 880 Hz.
99fab31849: **Wavelength**: inversely related to frequency. Low notes have longer wavelengths, travel further and bend around obstacles more easily; high notes have shorter wavelengths and are more directional. That's why the next room always hears the bass first.
4e1dbe5f61: **2. The basics of how sound is amplified** (compared with a guitar)
633117dfe8: The place you sing (the bathroom sounds so good thanks to the reflections)
03416cd068: With strings alone, a guitar sounds faint and thin. The voice is the same: the vocal folds are just a pair of tissues a few millimetres long and rely on the resonating spaces to amplify them.
4a74dda576: **Pitch**: the first thing listeners notice is singing off pitch.
ee145a7a1f: **Tone**: what lets listeners recognise your voice.
6b8993174c: **Tempo and rhythm**: how steady you are with the accompaniment; rushing or dragging both make the whole song lose its centre.
287d5f022a: **4. The three basic elements of singing** (the backbone of this course)
a9db65720c: Breath is the fuel of singing
886f8cccdf: Resonance is the amplifier of singing
5b95a16033: Diction lets listeners follow the story
abb6c29b92: **5. The three basic elements of music**
b57cf3cc18: **Melody**: the main line the singer sings.
8042190cf8: **Harmony**: the colour the guitar chords provide; when singers understand the chords, their pitch has something to lean on.
e2000e6420: **Rhythm**: the song's groove, which you can recognise from the guitar's strumming and fingerpicking.
3a06600280: Note: the pie chart in the original notes spelled them "Hamonic" and "Rythem"; the correct spellings are Harmony and Rhythm.
17c445a104: **6. What makes a good lead singer**
32d50fc406: **Control**: volume, tone and emotion all rise and fall at will.
f5e33e1da0: **Stamina**: a show has 10 to 15 songs, and the last should sound as good as the first.
fcac81fb01: **Resolution**: the resolution of the voice, in other words the singer's character. Listeners know it's you from a single line; Lesson 5's "hook" goes into this further.
e4f4e228e7: Extended notes: the pop song formula
e8efae0309: Most pop songs are built on the same formula: intro → verse → pre-chorus → chorus → after the interlude, back to the verse; after the second chorus comes the bridge, then back to the chorus and the outro. Once you understand each section's role, you can plan how to spend your energy and emotion.
6108adabc0: Listen carefully for the starting note, settle your breathing, get ready for the first line
40a25a855b: Tells the story in a mid-to-low range
2840aacb81: Close to a speaking voice, clear diction, holding back about 30% of the volume
cadf240b36: Gradually use more air, building energy for the chorus
49f2093b53: The song's centre and its hook
8fe81a289c: The fullest resonance and strongest emotion, and where the highest note is
e36efa4d77: Have a sip of water, reset your breath, get ready for round two
73184b3713: A turn in melody or mood
080a875219: Change tone or intensity so the last chorus hits harder
9161e9eee2: Repeats or extends the last line
9a34814d00: You can change the rhythm or slow down to let it linger
9ef2d1c33f: Close the sound cleanly and let the last note fade
c10bccc75f: **Example: PiA Chiu 《太陽》** (Lesson 2 practice song): intro → verse ▲ "你總感到落寞沮喪" → chorus ★ "我只想做你的太陽" → after the interlude, back to ▲ → ★ → bridge "也許有一天你不再記得我" → back to ★ → outro. The bridge comes in on an F chord, against the verse and chorus that start on C. That contrast is the clearest signal of a "turn".
